title: "I Will Fight No More Forever"
text:
In 1877 the United States government ordered the non-treaty bands of the Nez Perce to leave their homeland in the Wallowa Valley of Oregon and move to a reservation in Idaho. Shortly before the deadline, some young warriors killed several settlers, and the army attacked. Joseph, called Hinmatoowyalahtqit, was one of several band leaders.

For almost four months about seven hundred and fifty Nez Perce, most of them women, children and old people, retreated across Idaho, Wyoming and Montana, more than a thousand miles, fighting off pursuing army columns. They were heading for Canada.

At the Bear Paw Mountains in Montana, about forty miles from the border, Colonel Nelson Miles's troops caught and surrounded them. After a siege of several days in snow and cold, on October 5, 1877, Joseph surrendered. Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood recorded the message he said Joseph sent: that the chiefs were killed, the old men were dead, the little children were freezing, and his people had no blankets and no food. It ended: "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

The army's promise that they could return home was broken. The survivors were sent to Kansas and then Indian Territory.
lesson: When pride and the survival of the people you lead pull in different directions, choosing their survival is not defeat but responsibility.
people: Chief Joseph (Hinmatoowyalahtqit), Nelson Miles, Charles Erskine Scott Wood
source: Surrender speech as reported by Lt. Charles Erskine Scott Wood; army reports of the Nez Perce campaign
caveat: Wood later wrote the speech down and may have shaped its wording; whether Joseph spoke these exact words is debated.
